title: Meet the under-35s shaping the future of biotech
gist: A tour of five biotech researchers from MIT Technology Review's 35 Innovators Under 35 list, each anchored to a concrete result: a $70 Tanzanian postpartum-hemorrhage wrap that stopped bleeding in 73% of women within 20 minutes, neuron-like flexible brain electrodes and kirigami-inspired electrode sheets, the bespoke gene-editing therapy dosed into infant KJ Muldoon at seven months, partial-reprogramming age reversal now in human trials at Life Biosciences (first volunteer dosed June), and generative-AI-designed bacteriophages that replicated and infected bacteria. The through-line is that cheap devices, personalized gene editing, epigenetic reprogramming and generative biology have all crossed from paper to dosed patients or working wet-lab demonstrations.

insights.claim: Postpartum hemorrhage contributes to roughly 29% of maternal deaths in Tanzania, concentrating a large share of maternal mortality in a single, mechanically treatable complication.
insights.speaker: Jessica Hamzelou
insights.so_what: A single failure mode driving ~29% of deaths means a cheap device can capture an outsized share of the achievable mortality reduction — the kind of concentrated target global-health funders and impact investors pay for.
insights.quote: a dangerous birth complication that contributes to around 29% of maternal deaths in his home country, Tanzania

insights.claim: The Mkanda Salama ("Safe Wrap") device, developed by 28-year-old Paschal Kija, costs just $70 and was found in a study to stop postpartum bleeding in 73% of women within 20 minutes.
insights.speaker: Jessica Hamzelou
insights.so_what: A $70 unit price with a 73%/20-minute efficacy readout is a procurement-ready economics profile — watch for NGO and ministry-of-health bulk orders rather than a conventional venture exit path.
insights.quote: The Mkanda Salama (“Safe Wrap” in Swahili) is easy to use and costs just $70. A study found that it stopped postpartum bleeding in 73% of women within 20 minutes.

insights.claim: Ease of use is presented as a design requirement on par with efficacy for the low-cost hemorrhage device, implying the binding constraint in low-resource obstetric care is trained-operator availability rather than device performance.
insights.speaker: Jessica Hamzelou
insights.so_what: Device businesses targeting low-resource settings are won on training burden and unit cost, not clinical superiority — screen portfolio companies on those axes.
insights.locator: The Mkanda Salama ("Safe Wrap" in Swahili)

insights.claim: Brain electrodes have been developed, tested and implanted for decades, but because they are physically inserted into the brain they can cause damage to surrounding tissue — a persistent tradeoff between diagnostic and therapeutic value and injury.
insights.speaker: Jessica Hamzelou
insights.so_what: Tissue damage is the durability ceiling on implanted neural interfaces; materials fixes, not electronics, determine how long a brain-computer interface can stay implanted and therefore its addressable market.
insights.quote: These devices are literally inserted into people’s brains, so while they can help us understand brain activity and treat various neurological disorders, it’s not totally surprising that they can also cause a bit of damage.
insights.locator: 2. Making brain electrodes inspired by Japanese art

insights.claim: Xiao Yang, 34, is building ultra-small flexible brain electrodes that physically resemble actual neurons, on the thesis that matching the scale and mechanical compliance of native tissue reduces implantation damage.
insights.speaker: Jessica Hamzelou
insights.so_what: Biomimetic compliance is the emerging differentiator in neural interfaces — a technical axis on which incumbent rigid-probe implant players could be leapfrogged.
insights.quote: Her electrodes are flexible, too—in fact, they look a lot like actual neurons.
insights.locator: Xiao Yang, 34, is working on ultra-small electrodes

insights.claim: Kirigami, the traditional Japanese art of cutting paper into three-dimensional shapes, has been adapted into a honeycombed, spiral-basket-shaped sheet of electrodes already in use for studying brain cells in the lab.
insights.speaker: Jessica Hamzelou
insights.so_what: Borrowing fabrication geometry from paper-cutting turns 2D lithography into cheap 3D recording arrays — a cost path for lab tools and organoid instrumentation vendors.
insights.quote: Inspired by kirigami—the traditional Japanese art of cutting paper to form three-dimensional shapes—she’s created a sheet of electrodes with a honeycombed structure shaped like a spiral basket.
insights.locator: Yang is also creating sheets of electrodes

insights.claim: A bespoke gene-editing therapy was designed, screened, tested in mice and monkeys, and dosed into a single infant — Kyle "KJ" Muldoon Jr., born in 2024 with a rare, potentially fatal genetic disorder — by the time he was about seven months old.
insights.speaker: Jessica Hamzelou
insights.so_what: A roughly seven-month concept-to-dose timeline for a one-patient therapy implies the rate limiter for personalized medicine is now regulatory and manufacturing throughput, not biology.
insights.quote: KJ ultimately got his first dose of the resulting treatment when he was about seven months old.
insights.locator: 3. Developing an all-new treatment for baby KJ

insights.claim: The development workflow for the personalized therapy was to engineer cells carrying the patient's own genetic variant, use them to screen candidate gene-editing approaches, then test the leading medicines in mice and monkeys — a repeatable template rather than a one-off improvisation.
insights.speaker: Jessica Hamzelou
insights.so_what: A standardized patient-variant-in-a-dish screening pipeline is the platform layer that makes n-of-1 editing investable; look for CDMOs and screening-tool vendors positioned under it.
insights.quote: Grandinette, who is now 26, created cells with KJ’s genetic variant and used them to screen gene-editing approaches; then she tested potential medicines in mice and monkeys.
insights.locator: Sarah Grandinette was a member of a team

insights.claim: The patient treated with the personalized gene-editing therapy responded well, was discharged from hospital, and is reported to be doing pretty great — a positive clinical outcome rather than merely a technical demonstration.
insights.speaker: Jessica Hamzelou
insights.so_what: A durable good outcome in the field's flagship n-of-1 case is what unlocks regulatory precedent and payer conversations for bespoke editing.
insights.locator: He responded well and was eventually discharged

insights.claim: The buzziest technology in longevity is reprogramming — attempts to rewind the age of cells by resetting them toward a more embryonic-like state — making cell-age reversal, not senolytics or metabolic drugs, the field's current center of gravity.
insights.speaker: Jessica Hamzelou
insights.so_what: Capital and talent in longevity are concentrating on reprogramming; it sets the valuation comps and the scientific risk that the whole sector now shares.
insights.quote: The buzziest tech in longevity right now centers on reprogramming—attempts to rewind the age of cells by resetting them to a more embryonic-like state.
insights.locator: 4. Reversing the aging process to treat eye disease

insights.claim: A reprogramming therapy shown in a 2020 study to reverse vision loss in aged, blind mice has advanced to an almost identical version now being tested in humans with eye disease, with Life Biosciences dosing its first volunteer in June.
insights.speaker: Jessica Hamzelou
insights.so_what: First-in-human dosing turns age reversal from a preclinical story into a readout-driven catalyst — safety and early efficacy data from this trial is the single most important datapoint for the reprogramming thesis.
insights.quote: Life Biosciences, the company developing the drug, dosed its first volunteer in June.

insights.claim: Age-reversal technology is entering the clinic through eye disease rather than systemic aging, using the eye as a contained, locally dosable organ to de-risk a therapy whose systemic version carries cancer and dedifferentiation concerns.
insights.speaker: Jessica Hamzelou
insights.so_what: Expect the reprogramming sector's regulatory path to be organ-by-organ starting with the eye; systemic anti-aging claims remain years and several safety hurdles away.
insights.locator: Now an almost identical version of that therapy

insights.claim: The roughly six-year gap between the 2020 mouse vision-restoration result and the first human dose illustrates the realistic translation lag for reprogramming therapies.
insights.speaker: Jessica Hamzelou
insights.so_what: Use a multi-year mouse-to-human lag as the base rate when underwriting today's preclinical longevity announcements.

insights.claim: A generative AI model was used to produce entirely new genetic blueprints for bacteriophages, which were then printed as DNA strands, and in experiments the AI-designed viruses replicated, burst out of bacterial cells, and infected nearby bacteria.
insights.speaker: Jessica Hamzelou
insights.so_what: Working AI-designed viral genomes prove the generative-biology loop closes end to end — a direct demand driver for DNA synthesis capacity and a trigger for biosecurity screening rules.
insights.quote: he found that those AI-designed viruses could create new copies of themselves, burst out of bacterial cells, and infect other nearby bacteria
insights.locator: 5. Using AI to design new viruses

insights.claim: The proposed applications for AI-designed life forms are making drugs and soaking up pollution, positioning generative biology as an industrial-biomanufacturing and environmental-remediation play rather than only a therapeutics one.
insights.speaker: Jessica Hamzelou
insights.so_what: Widens the addressable market narrative for generative-biology startups beyond pharma into chemicals and environmental services — but the framing is aspirational, so discount accordingly.
insights.quote: King, 27, hopes that AI-designed life forms might one day be used to make drugs or soak up pollution

insights.claim: The distinction that viruses are not alive is invoked explicitly when describing AI-designed organisms, signaling that the field is already managing the framing of how far generative models have gone toward designing life.
insights.speaker: Jessica Hamzelou
insights.so_what: The definitional hedge is a leading indicator of coming public and regulatory scrutiny of AI-designed organisms — a policy risk to price into synthetic-biology exposure.

insights.claim: Nine of the 35 people on MIT Technology Review's 2026 Innovators Under 35 list work in biotech, and the five profiled cluster into low-cost devices, neural interfaces, personalized gene editing, cellular reprogramming and AI-designed organisms.
insights.speaker: Jessica Hamzelou
insights.so_what: Where a curated young-talent list concentrates is a cheap proxy for where the next decade's founding teams and venture rounds will form — these five buckets are the map.
insights.quote: This year, the list includes nine people who are transforming biotech.

insights.claim: Three of the five profiled researchers are under 30 — ages 26, 27 and 28 — and are already credited with dosed therapies, deployed devices and working synthetic organisms, indicating that frontier biotech results are being produced very early in careers.
insights.speaker: Jessica Hamzelou
insights.so_what: Falling cost of biological tooling is compressing the experience threshold for meaningful results — supports seed-stage bets on very young technical founders in bio.
